newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: 50,000 in Belgrade demo despite police threat.
newsitem.headline: 50,000 in Belgrade demo despite police threat.

text.p: Fifty thousand students and opposition supporters demonstrated against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday as international protests grew against his threats to quell street unrest with force.

Demonstrators marched through central Belgrade in a snow storm, taunting police deployed in small numbers despite an official warning that security forces would be less tolerant of anti-government protests that have lasted more than two weeks.
Opposition leaders said the turnout was a blow to the regime's hopes of quelling the protests by intimidation.

"Today the people of Belgrade defended the city after the Serbian parliament speaker offended Belgraders by calling them fascists," Vuk Draskovic of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition told the crowd.
"These demonstrations will continue ... if there is any provocation, we will answer peacefully by sitting and by song."
The daily demonstrations began against alleged socialist rigging of elections last month but have grown into demands for the ouster of Milosevic after nine years in power.
The opposition accused the president and his formerly communist Socialist party of running a one-party state disguised as a multi-party democracy.

Zoran Djindjic, another Zajedno leader, said: "We are here because we will not recognise the votes that have been stolen from us but also because we do not accept anything else (the socialists) have robbed us of -- our history, our dignity our money."
Britain and France, reflecting international alarm at threat to send in the police, urged Milosevic to show restraint.
"We call on the Serbian authorities to respect the democratic right of peaceful demonstration without qualification," a Foreign Office statement said in London.

A line of girls led Monday's demonstration, handing carnations to policemen along the march route. One policeman accepted the flower and stuck it in his flak jacket but most, watched by vigilant officers, refused.
The students blew trumpets and waved football rattles to create maximum uproar as they weaved through the city gathering support.

"They teach us to think for ourselves at university but now Slobo and his mates expect us to switch off our brains when they speak," a philosophy student said. "Only a five-year-old would be fooled by this."
With no sign of the protests flagging, political sources said the government was desperately seeking an escape route but was running out of options to save face.

It cancelled a Serbian parliament session on Tuesday when the Zajedno was due to demand that the disputed elections be set aside. It threatened to boycott of parliament if the results were allowed to stand, robbing it of victories it claimed in Belgrade and other cities.
The danger of police intervention in the dispute in Belgrade caused concern in Montenegro, Serbia's junior partner in the Yugoslav federation.

Montenegrin media quoted Svetozar Marovic, socialist speaker of the Montenegrin parliament, as saying: "It is very important ... that those who take care of the people and of the state keep a cool and rational head."
The rolling protests have attracted up to 100,000 people on some days in a challenge which is steadily eroding Milosevic's authority and reputation as a political master tactician.

The autocratic Serbian leader, rarely seen in public, has stayed out of sight during the protests and held back his 100,000-strong police force in contrast with tough measures to stifle previous unrest against his rule.
He used tanks to smash demonstrations in 1991 and riot police were deployed quickly in the past to counter any whiff of trouble.
Zajedno and student leaders have stopped the stoning of state television and newspaper buildings that marred earlier protests in order to deprive police of any excuse to intervene.
Police said they had arrested 23 people for causing damage or disruption since the demonstrations began.

The socialists have tried to deny publicity for the protests, jamming independent radio B-92's signal although it was on the air on Monday. The radio gave out its e-mail address to listeners in case it was jammed again.
